stem: A fair four-sided die (faces 1 to 4) and a fair five-sided die (faces 1 to 5) are rolled, and $X$ is the larger of the two results (either one if they tie). What is $P(X = 4)$?

options.why: This counts only the outcomes where the four-sided die shows 4; a 4 on the five-sided die with a smaller value on the other die also gives a maximum of 4.
This is $P(X\le4)$, the probability that the maximum does not exceed 4.
This is the probability that the four-sided die shows 4, not the probability that the maximum is 4.

solution: Maximum at most 4: both dice at most 4: $4\times4 = 16$ outcomes. Maximum at most 3: $3\times3 = 9$ outcomes.
hints: Count the outcomes where the maximum equals 4 exactly.
Use $P(X\le4)-P(X\le3)$.
The sample space has $4\times5 = 20$ equally likely outcomes.
concept: Probability mass function of a maximum.
why: The event $\{X=4\}$ is the difference of two nested "at most" events.

sub: rank of the best of a group
stem: Two senior and two junior analysts are ranked by a panel; all $4! = 24$ rankings are equally likely. Let $X$ be the rank of the best-placed junior (rank 1 is best). What is $P(X = 2)$?

options.why: This is $P(X=1)$, the probability that a junior is top ranked.
This is the probability that the second-ranked person is a junior given a senior is first; it must be multiplied by the probability that a senior is first.
This is $P(X=3)$: both seniors fill ranks 1 and 2.

solution: $X=2$ means rank 1 is a senior and rank 2 is a junior.
hints: What must be true of ranks 1 and 2 for the best junior to be second?
Multiply conditional probabilities for the first two ranks.
After a senior is first, 2 juniors remain among 3 people.
concept: Distribution of the position of the first success in random order.
misconception: Omitting the conditioning on the first rank.
why: The event is a specific sequence of types in the first two positions.

stem: A broker makes two independent trades. The first is profitable with probability 0.5, the second with probability 0.4. A profitable trade yields \$100 or \$200 with equal probability; an unprofitable trade yields \$0. Let $X$ be the total gain. What is $P(X = 200)$?

options.why: This is only the case in which both trades are profitable with \$100 each.
This includes the single-profit cases only; both trades yielding \$100 also gives \$200.
This is the probability that both trades are profitable, which includes totals of 200, 300 and 400.

solution: Total \$200 can arise in three disjoint ways:
hints: List the ways in which the two gains can sum to \$200.
Include the cases in which one trade is unprofitable.
Multiply independent probabilities within each case and add the cases.
concept: Distribution of a sum of independent discrete gains.
why: The three cases are disjoint, so their probabilities add.

stem: A university has three lecture sections with 20, 30 and 70 students. A student is chosen at random from all 120 students and $X$ is the size of that student's section. What is $E[X]$?

options.why: This averages over sections (a randomly chosen section), not over students.
This is the size of the largest section; students are spread over all three sections.
This divides the number of students by the number of students and has no relation to the average section size seen by a student.

hints: Which is chosen at random: a section or a student?
A section is selected with probability proportional to its size.
Weight each section size by its share of students.
misconception: Averaging section sizes with equal weights.
why: Large sections hold more students, so a random student is more likely to be in one.

stem: An insurer pays \$80,000 if a claim occurs within a year; the claim probability is 0.015. The premium $P$ is set so that the insurer's expected profit equals 20% of the premium. What premium should be charged?

options.why: This premium covers the expected payout only and leaves zero expected profit.
This adds 20% of the expected payout as profit, but the profit must be 20% of the premium.
This reduces the expected payout, which gives an expected loss.

solution: Expected profit $= P - 0.015(80000) = P-1200$. Set this equal to $0.2P$: $0.8P = 1200$, so $P = 1500$.
hints: Write the expected profit in terms of the premium.
The target is 20% of the premium, not of the claim cost.
Solve the linear equation.
misconception: Taking a percentage of the wrong base.
why: The premium appears on both sides of the profit equation.

stem: A committee of 5 is chosen at random from 12 employees, 4 of whom are women. What is the expected number of women on the committee?

options.why: This is the proportion of women, not the expected count for a committee of 5.
The probability that a given member is a woman is $4/12$, not $4/11$.
This assumes half the committee are women.

solution: Each of the 5 seats is held by a woman with probability $4/12$ (by symmetry).
hints: Use an indicator for each committee member.
What is the probability that a given committee member is a woman?
Add the expectations.
concept: Expectation of a hypergeometric count by linearity.
misconception: Using a binomial formula with the wrong probability.
why: Each position is equally likely to be any employee.

sub: expected value of a betting strategy
stem: A gambler bets on an event of probability 0.45 at even odds. Strategy: stake \$1; if it wins, stop. If it loses, stake \$2; if that wins, stop. If that loses, stake \$4 and then stop whatever happens. Let $X$ be the net gain. What is $E[X]$?

options.why: Even odds would give zero expectation only if the event had probability 0.5.
The final loss is \$7 (1+2+4), not \$1.
This is the expectation of a single \$1 bet; the strategy has several stages.

solution: Wins: stage 1: $+1$ with prob $0.45$; stage 2: $-1+2 = +1$ with prob $0.55\cdot0.45$; stage 3: $-1-2+4 = +1$ with prob $0.55^2\cdot0.45$. All three lost: $-1-2-4 = -7$ with prob $0.55^3 = 0.1664$.
hints: Enumerate the four outcomes of the strategy and the gain in each.
Compute the probability of each branch.
Weight the gains and add.
misconception: Assuming a staking system beats an unfavourable game.
why: Frequent small wins are offset by rare large losses; expectation stays negative.

stem: A prize is hidden in one of 12 boxes, each equally likely. Boxes are opened one at a time in a fixed order until the prize is found. What is the expected number of boxes opened?

options.why: This is the midpoint of 0 to 12; the first box is box number 1, so the mean is $(1+12)/2$.
This is the worst case, when the prize is in the last box.
This is the probability that the prize is in any particular box.

solution: The number of boxes opened equals the position $K$ of the prize, uniform on $1,\dots,12$.
hints: What is the distribution of the position of the prize?
Use the sum $1+2+\cdots+n = n(n+1)/2$.
Divide the sum of the positions by 12.
concept: Expectation of a discrete uniform variable.
misconception: Using $n/2$ for a variable starting at 1.
why: The mean of a discrete uniform variable on $1..n$ is $(n+1)/2$.

stem: Sixty blood samples are split into ten batches of six and each batch is mixed and tested once. A mixed batch tests positive if any of its samples is positive, and each sample is independently positive with probability 0.05. Positive batches are then re-tested sample by sample (six more tests); negative batches need nothing more. What is the expected total number of tests?

options.why: This counts only the pooled tests; positive pools require 6 additional tests.
This is the number of tests with no pooling.
The probability that a pool is positive is $1-0.95^6$, not $6\times0.05$ scaled again.

solution: Each pool needs 1 test, plus 6 more if positive. $P(\text{positive}) = 1-0.95^6 \approx 0.2649$.
hints: How many tests does a single pool need in each case?
What is the probability that a pool of 6 is positive?
Multiply the expected tests per pool by 10.
concept: Expected cost of a conditional procedure.
why: Pooling pays off when positives are rare.

stem: A bakery bakes $k$ loaves each morning at a cost of \$2 each and sells them at \$5; unsold loaves are worthless. Daily demand is equally likely to be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 loaves. How many loaves should it bake to maximise expected profit?

options.why: At $k=3$ the expected profit is 6.5, below the 7.0 obtained with 4 loaves.
Baking for the maximum demand wastes loaves on low-demand days: the expected profit is 5.5, below the optimum.
At $k=2$ the expected profit is about 5.17, well below the optimum.

solution: Profit for $k$ loaves and demand $d$ is $5\min(d,k)-2k$. Averaging over $d=1,\dots,6$ gives expected profits $k=1$: 3.00; $k=2$: 5.17; $k=3$: 6.50; $k=4$: 7.00; $k=5$: 6.67; $k=6$: 5.50.
Equivalently, loaf number $k$ sells with probability $(7-k)/6$ and is worth baking while $5(7-k)/6 > 2$, i.e. $k\le4$.
hints: Compute the expected profit for each order quantity $k$.
Think about the marginal loaf: probability it sells times \$5 minus its \$2 cost.
Order while the marginal expected gain is positive.
concept: Optimising expected profit over a discrete decision.
misconception: Ordering for the average or maximum demand.
why: The optimum balances the cost of unsold loaves against forgone sales.

stem: A box holds 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. You win \$3 if they are the same colour and lose \$2 if they differ. What is your expected winning?

options.why: The probability of the same colour is $21/45$, not 0.52.
This averages the two prizes with equal weights; the outcomes are not equally likely.
This ignores the loss on the differing-colour outcomes.

hints: Find the probability of two marbles of the same colour.
The complement is "different colours".
Weight the gain and the loss by these probabilities.
concept: Expected value of a two-outcome game.
why: Expected value weights each payoff by its probability.

stem: A bank has four branches with 12, 18, 30 and 40 staff. One branch is chosen at random (each with probability $\tfrac14$) and $Y$ is its staff count. What is $\mathrm{Var}(Y)$?

options.why: This is the standard deviation, not the variance.
This is $E[Y^2]$; the square of the mean must be subtracted.
This divides by 3 as for a sample variance; here the four branches are the whole distribution.

hints: Find the mean of $Y$ first.
Then compute $E[Y^2]$.
Use $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = E[Y^2]-(E[Y])^2$.
why: The shortcut formula reduces variance to two expectations.

stem: A random variable $X$ has $E[X] = 2$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 3$. Find $E\big[(X-1)(X+3)\big]$.

options.why: This substitutes the mean into the product; $E[g(X)]\ne g(E[X])$ for a quadratic.
The linear term $2X$ was dropped when expanding $(X-1)(X+3) = X^2+2X-3$.
The constant term has the wrong sign: $(X-1)(X+3)$ expands with $-3$, not $+3$.

hints: Expand the product.
Find $E[X^2]$ from the variance and the mean.
Use linearity of expectation on the expanded form.
misconception: Plugging the mean into a nonlinear expression.
why: Variance is exactly the gap between $E[X^2]$ and $(E[X])^2$.

stem: In a promotion a customer rolls a fair six-sided die and, separately, spins a fair two-sided token. The prize in dollars is three times the die value if the token lands on gold and half the die value if it lands on silver. What is the expected prize?

options.why: This is the expected die value alone, without the multipliers.
The multipliers must be weighted by the coin probabilities $\frac12$ each.
The expected multiplier is 1.75; it still has to be multiplied by the expected die value 3.5.

solution: The coin and die are independent: $E[\text{winnings}] = E[\text{multiplier}]\,E[\text{die}] = (0.5\cdot3+0.5\cdot0.5)(3.5) = 1.75\times3.5 = 6.125$.
hints: Find the expected multiplier from the coin.
The die value has expectation 3.5.
Independence lets you multiply the two expectations.
concept: Expectation of a product of independent variables.
misconception: Ignoring one of the two sources of randomness.
why: For independent factors $E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]$.

stem: Two reviewers each independently pick 4 of 15 papers at random. What is the expected number of papers picked by both reviewers?

options.why: This is one reviewer’s probability of picking a given paper, not the expected size of the overlap.
This is the expected number of papers picked by one reviewer.
This is the probability that one particular paper is picked by both reviewers; the expected count sums it over all 15 papers.

solution: For a given paper, $P(\text{picked by both}) = \dfrac4{15}\cdot\dfrac4{15}$ by independence.
hints: Define an indicator for each paper.
The two reviewers choose independently: multiply their selection probabilities.
Add over the 15 papers.
misconception: Counting papers rather than using probabilities.
why: Linearity avoids any need for the joint distribution of the count.

stem: 25 colleagues each independently pick one of the 12 calendar months at random for a holiday. What is the expected number of different months that are chosen?

options.why: With 25 people it is very likely, but not certain, that every month appears; the expectation is slightly below 12.
This is the expected number of months that nobody chooses.
This is the expected number of people per month, not the number of months chosen.

solution: For each month define an indicator that at least one person chooses it. $P = 1-(11/12)^{25} \approx 0.8866$.
hints: Define an indicator for each month.
The probability that nobody picks a given month is $(11/12)^{25}$.
Add the 12 expectations.
concept: Expected number of occupied categories via indicators.
misconception: Trying to find the full distribution.
why: Linearity makes the dependence between months irrelevant.

stem: A cereal brand includes one of 5 different collectible cards in every box, each type equally likely and independently of earlier boxes. What is the expected number of boxes needed to complete the set?

options.why: This is the number of different cards; repeats are expected before the set is complete.
The last card needs an expected $5/1 = 5$ boxes, which was left out of the sum.
This is $5^2$; the expected number is smaller because later stages need fewer cards.

solution: After $k$ distinct cards, each box yields a new one with probability $(5-k)/5$, so the wait is geometric with mean $5/(5-k)$.
hints: Split the collection into stages: waiting for the first new card, the second, and so on.
Each stage is a geometric waiting time.
Add the expected waiting times.
misconception: Assuming the number of boxes equals the number of cards.
why: The final cards take longest because few new types remain.

stem: Twelve independent rolls are made of a fair die with faces numbered 1 to 4, and the face values are added. Find the variance of this total.

options.why: This is the variance of one roll; the 12 independent variances add.
This is the sum of second moments, $12E[X^2]$, not the variance.
This would be the variance of 12 times a single roll (perfect dependence), not of a sum of 12 independent rolls.

hints: Find the variance of one roll first.
Are the rolls independent?
Add 12 equal variances.
concept: Variance of a sum of independent variables.
why: Independence removes covariances so only variances remain.

stem: A continuous variable has density $f(x) = c\,(4-x^2)$ for $-2<x<2$ and 0 elsewhere. What is $c$?

options.why: This integrates only over $(0,2)$, which is half the support.
This would normalise a constant density on $(-2,2)$; the $x^2$ term is ignored.
The integral is $32/3$, not $64/3$.

hints: A density must integrate to 1 over its support.
Integrate $4-x^2$ from $-2$ to $2$.
Divide 1 by the integral to solve for $c$.
misconception: Integrating over only half the support.
why: The constant $c$ scales the area under the curve to 1.

stem: A variable has density $f(x) = 2/x^3$ for $x>1$ and 0 otherwise. Which statement is correct?

answer.display: $E[X] = 2$ is finite, but $E[X^2]$ is infinite, so $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ does not exist

options.text: $E[X] = 2$ is finite, but $E[X^2]$ is infinite, so $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ does not exist

options.why: $E[X^2] = \int_1^\infty 2/x\,dx$ diverges logarithmically.
$E[X] = \int_1^\infty 2/x^2\,dx = 2$, which is finite.
The mean of this density is 2, and the variance is not finite.

solution: $E[X^2] = \int_1^\infty \dfrac{2}{x}dx = \infty$, so the variance does not exist.
hints: Compute $E[X]$ by integrating $x f(x)$.
Then check $E[X^2]$ by integrating $x^2 f(x)$.
Does $\int_1^\infty 1/x\,dx$ converge?
concept: Mean may exist while variance does not.
misconception: Assuming that a finite mean implies a finite variance.
why: The heavier the tail, the lower the highest moment that exists.

stem: A waiting time $X$ (in minutes) is described by a linear density $f(x) = a+bx$ on $0\le x\le2$ and zero elsewhere, and its mean is known to be $1.2$ minutes. Find the probability that the wait exceeds one minute.

options.why: This would hold for a symmetric density; here the mean 1.2 exceeds 1 but the density is not constant.
This is $P(X<1) = a + b/2$, the complement of the probability asked for.
This is $E[X]/2$, not a tail probability.

solution: Subtract twice the first from... solving gives $b = 0.3$, $a = 0.2$.
hints: Use two conditions: total probability 1 and the given mean.
Solve the two linear equations for $a$ and $b$.
Integrate the density from 1 to 2.
concept: Determining a density from moment conditions.
misconception: Forgetting one of the two conditions.
why: Two unknown parameters need two conditions.

stem: The lifetime (in years) of a component has density $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{4}\,e^{-x/2}$ for $x\ge0$. What is its expected lifetime?

options.why: This is the mean of the density $x e^{-x}$, which has a different scale.
This is $2\times$ the mean; the scale parameter is 2 and the shape is 2, giving a mean of 4.
This is not obtained from the integral of $x f(x)$.

solution: (This is a gamma distribution with shape 2 and scale 2: mean $2\times2 = 4$.)
hints: Set up $\int_0^\infty x f(x)\,dx$.
Substitute $x = 2u$ to reach a standard gamma integral.
Use $\int_0^\infty u^n e^{-u}du = n!$.
concept: Mean of a continuous distribution by integration.
why: Rescaling the variable multiplies the mean by the scale.

stem: Option $A$ pays \$0, \$3 or \$12 with probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. Option $B$ pays \$0, \$1 or \$15 with probabilities 0.6, 0.25 and 0.15. Which option has the higher expected payoff?

options.text: Option $B$: it offers the largest single prize, \$15
options.why: The expected payoff of $B$ is $0.25+2.25 = \$2.50$, below $A$’s \$3.30.

options.text: They are equal, since both have a 50% to 60% chance of paying nothing
options.why: The chance of paying nothing is different, and so are the expected payoffs.

solution: Option $A$ has the higher expected payoff.
hints: Compute the expected payoff of each option separately.
A zero payoff contributes nothing to the expectation.
Compare the two values.
concept: Using expected value to compare options.
why: Expectation summarises each distribution with a single number weighted by probability.

stem: A call centre expects 340 calls on a given day. 15% of calls are complaints and 20% of complaints are escalated to a manager. About how many calls are expected to be escalated?

options.why: This is the expected number of complaints, not the escalated ones.
The 20% applies only to complaints, not to all calls.
The proportions are applied in sequence (multiplied), not added.

hints: How many of the calls are complaints?
The escalation rate applies to complaints only.
Multiply the proportions.
why: Each proportion is a conditional rate applied in turn.

stem: The number $X$ of defects found on a circuit board has pmf $p(0)=0.30$, $p(1)=0.30$, $p(2)=0.20$, $p(3)=0.12$, $p(4)=0.08$. What is $P(1\le X\le3)$?

options.why: The value $X=0$ (probability 0.30) is not in the interval.
This is $P(1<X<3) = P(X=2)$; the end values 1 and 3 are included.
The value $X=4$ lies outside the interval.

hints: Which values of $X$ satisfy $1\le X\le3$?
The end points are included.
Add their probabilities.
concept: Probabilities of events defined by a discrete variable.
misconception: Excluding or including the wrong end points.
why: A discrete event’s probability is the sum of the pmf over its values.

stem: Which of the following is a valid probability mass function?

options.why: The probabilities sum to $15/10 = 1.5 > 1$.
$p(1) = -1/6$ is negative.
The probabilities sum to $55/50 > 1$.

solution: $(6-x)/15$ for $x=1,\dots,5$ gives $5,4,3,2,1$ over 15: all non-negative and summing to $15/15 = 1$.
The other candidates violate non-negativity or sum to more than 1.
hints: Check non-negativity for each candidate.
Then check whether the probabilities sum to 1.
Only one candidate satisfies both.
why: Probabilities must be non-negative and total 1.

stem: The annual loss from a fire is \$0, \$2,000 or \$8,000 with probabilities 0.85, 0.10 and 0.05. An insurer pays the loss in excess of a \$1,000 deductible. What premium gives the insurer an expected profit of \$150?

options.why: This ignores the deductible and prices as if the insurer paid the whole loss.
This is the expected payout; the target profit of \$150 has not been added.
The profit must be added to, not subtracted from, the expected payout.

solution: Payout: \$1,000 with probability 0.10 and \$7,000 with probability 0.05.
hints: What does the insurer pay in each loss case after the deductible?
Compute the expected payout.
Add the required expected profit.
concept: Expected value of a policy payout.
why: Expected profit is premium minus expected payout.

stem: A warehouse holds 100 units and ships them in crates of 4. The number of crates $X$ ordered has variance $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 2.25$. What is the variance of the number of units left after the order, $Y = 100-4X$?

options.why: The coefficient must be squared when scaling a variance: $a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$.
Multiplying by 4 scales the variance by 16; only the constant 100 leaves it unchanged.
The constant 100 does not multiply the variance; it has no effect on it.

hints: Which part of $100-4X$ affects the variance?
The coefficient is squared.
Multiply $(-4)^2$ by 2.25.
why: Shifts change location, not spread; scalings change spread quadratically.

stem: Two fair four-sided dice (faces 1 to 4) are rolled and $M$ is the larger of the two results. What is $E[M]$?

options.why: This is the mean of a single die; the maximum of two is larger on average.
This is $E[\min]$, the expected smaller value.
This is the largest possible value of the maximum, not its expectation.

hints: Find $P(M\le k)$ for each $k$ and difference them.
Write the pmf of $M$.
Compute $\sum k\,P(M=k)$.
misconception: Assuming the maximum has the same mean as one die.
why: Taking a maximum shifts probability towards large values.

stem: $X$ is uniform on $\{1,3,5\}$ and $Y$ is uniform on $\{0,2,4\}$, independently. What is $P(X+Y\ge7)$?

options.why: This is $P(X+Y\ge5)$, which includes the sums 5.
This is only the sum 9; the sums 7 also qualify.
There are 9 equally likely pairs; 3 give a sum of at least 7.

solution: The nine pairs are equally likely. Sums $\ge7$: $(3,4)\to7$, $(5,2)\to7$, $(5,4)\to9$: 3 pairs.
hints: How many equally likely pairs are there?
List the pairs with sum at least 7.
Divide the favourable count by the nine equally likely pairs.
concept: Probability of an event defined by a sum.
why: Independence and uniformity make the pairs equally likely.

stem: The number of failures in a week has pmf $f(x) = \dfrac{2}{(x+2)(x+3)}$ for $x = 0,1,2,\dots$ Find $P(X\ge3\mid X\ge1)$.

options.why: This is $P(X\ge3)$, which has not been divided by $P(X\ge1)$.
This is $P(X\ge1)$, the probability of the conditioning event.
There is no reason for the conditional probability to be one half.

solution: Write $f(x) = 2\left[\dfrac1{x+2}-\dfrac1{x+3}\right]$. The tail sum telescopes: $P(X\ge k) = \dfrac{2}{k+2}$.
hints: Use partial fractions on $f(x)$.
Sum the tail $\sum_{x\ge k}f(x)$: most terms cancel.
Since $\{X\ge3\}\subset\{X\ge1\}$, divide the two tail probabilities.
misconception: Not dividing by the conditioning probability.
why: The partial-fraction form turns the infinite sum into one remaining term.

sub: diagnose: expectation of a nonlinear function
stem: A firm’s monthly demand $X$ is equally likely to be 10 or 30 units. Revenue is $R = X^2$ (in thousands). A student says: "$E[X]=20$, so $E[R] = 20^2 = 400$." What is the error and the correct expected revenue?

options.why: For a nonlinear function, $E[g(X)] \neq g(E[X])$ in general; here $E[X^2] = \text{Var}(X) + (E[X])^2 = 100 + 400 = 500$.
Squaring is not linear; doubling is not the same as squaring.
Taking a square root reverses a square on the mean but does not give $E[X^2]$.

solution: Also $E[X^2] = \mathrm{Var}(X)+(E[X])^2 = 100 + 400$. The difference from 400 is the variance.
hints: Is squaring a linear operation?
Compute $E[X^2]$ directly from the two possible values.
How is $E[X^2]$ related to $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ and $(E[X])^2$?
concept: Expectation of a function of a random variable; variance as the gap.
misconception: Plugging the mean into a nonlinear function.
why: Variability raises the expected value of a convex function.

stem: Daily demand for a bakery’s special loaf has the distribution: 0 loaves (0.1), 10 (0.3), 20 (0.4), 30 (0.2). What is the expected daily demand?
hints: Multiply each demand by its probability.
Do not average the four demand values equally.
Add the four products.
misconception: Taking the plain average of the values.
why: Likelier values carry more weight.

stem: Using the demand distribution 0 (0.1), 10 (0.3), 20 (0.4), 30 (0.2), what is the variance of daily demand?
hints: Compute $E[X^2]$ with the same probabilities.
Subtract the square of the mean.
The mean is 17.
misconception: Squaring the expected value of $X$ only.
why: Variance is the mean square minus the squared mean.

sub: linear transformation of mean and variance
stem: Weekly cost $C$ (in thousands) has mean 12 and standard deviation 3. Cost in rupees is $Y = 1000\,C + 5000$. What is the standard deviation of $Y$?
solution: Adding a constant does not change spread; scaling by 1000 multiplies the standard deviation by 1000.
hints: Does adding 5000 change variability?
How does multiplying by 1000 change the SD?
Combine the effect of the shift and the scale.
concept: Shifts do not change spread; scales multiply it.
why: The SD scales by the absolute value of the multiplier.

stem: A shop has 8 customers waiting. Each independently buys with probability 0.35. Each purchase earns ₹120. What is the expected revenue?
hints: Write the count of purchases as a sum of indicators.
Expectation of a sum is the sum of expectations.
Multiply by the revenue per purchase.
why: Each customer contributes $0.35\times120$ on average.

stem: Ten employees each draw a name at random from a hat (without replacement) in a gift swap. What is the expected number of employees who draw their own name?
solution: Each person draws their own name with probability $1/10$.
By linearity (dependence does not matter) the expected count is $10\times1/10 = 1$.
hints: Define an indicator for each person.
What is each indicator’s probability?
Linearity does not need independence.
misconception: Trying to compute the full derangement distribution.
why: The answer 1 does not depend on the number of people.

stem: Two independent project costs have standard deviations 4 and 3 (in lakhs). What is the standard deviation of the total cost?
hints: Variances, not standard deviations, add for independent variables.
Square each SD first.
Take the square root of the sum.
why: Independent variability combines as a Pythagorean sum.

stem: Returns $X$ and $Y$ have $\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.04$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=0.09$ and correlation $\rho=-0.5$. What is the variance of the portfolio $X+Y$?
hints: Find the covariance from the correlation and SDs.
Use $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)$ with the covariance term.
Negative correlation reduces the total.
why: Negative covariance subtracts from the sum of variances.

stem: A raffle ticket costs ₹50. There is one prize of ₹5 000, two of ₹500 and the rest nothing; 200 tickets are sold. What is the expected net gain of one ticket?
hints: Total prize money divided by tickets gives the expected prize.
Subtract the ticket price.
A negative value means an expected loss.
why: The expected prize is below the ticket price.

stem: A vendor buys papers at ₹4 and sells at ₹7; unsold ones are worth nothing. Demand is 40 with probability 0.4 and 60 with probability 0.6. Which stock level (40 or 60) gives the higher expected profit?

options.text: 40 papers, because it never leaves unsold stock
options.why: Stock 40 gives a certain 120, which is lower than 132.

options.text: They give the same expected profit
options.why: Calculate: 120 against 132.

options.text: Neither: profit is negative either way
options.why: Both profits are positive.

hints: Compute profit for each demand under each stock level.
Weight by the demand probabilities.
Compare the expected profits.
concept: Choosing an order quantity by expected profit.
misconception: Choosing the safe option without computing.
why: The extra upside outweighs the cost of unsold stock.

stem: A non-negative integer variable $N$ has $P(N\ge1)=0.9$, $P(N\ge2)=0.5$, $P(N\ge3)=0.2$ and $P(N\ge4)=0$. What is $E[N]$?
hints: For non-negative integers, add up the tail probabilities.
Start the sum at $k=1$.
Add the three given values.
why: Each $k$ contributes $P(N\ge k)$.

stem: Customers are Retail (70%) with mean spend ₹800, or Corporate (30%) with mean spend ₹4 000. What is the overall mean spend per customer?
hints: Condition on the customer type.
Weight each mean by the type share.
Add the two weighted means together.
why: The rarer group has a large effect because of its high mean.

stem: A variable is $N(0,\,1)$ with probability 0.5 and $N(4,\,1)$ with probability 0.5 (mean, variance). What is its overall variance?
hints: Average the within-group variances.
Add the variance of the group means.
Group means are 0 and 4 with mean 2.
why: Mixtures are more spread out than their components.

stem: $X$ takes the values $-1, 0, 2$ with probabilities $0.3, 0.2, 0.5$. What is $E[X^2]$?
hints: Square each value first, then weight.
Do not square $E[X]$.
Add the weighted squares.
why: $E[X^2]\ne(E[X])^2$ unless the variance is zero.

stem: Two investments have the same mean annual return of 8%. Investment A has standard deviation 2%, B has 10%. What does this tell us?

answer.display: B’s returns are more spread out, so B is riskier in the sense of variability

options.text: B’s returns are more spread out, so B is riskier in the sense of variability
A has the higher average return
options.why: Both have the same mean of 8%.

options.text: B always returns more than A
options.why: Spread does not mean B is always higher.

options.text: The standard deviation says nothing about risk
options.why: It is a standard measure of variability.

solution: The mean describes the centre, the SD describes spread.
Same mean with a larger SD means more variability.
hints: Which number measures centre?
Which number measures spread?
Compare the SDs.
misconception: Equating a high SD with a high mean.
why: SD measures variability, not level.

sub: probability from a pmf with unknown constant
stem: A variable takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 with probabilities proportional to $k$, $2k$, $3k$, $4k$ for a constant $c$ such that $P(X=k)=ck$. What is $E[X]$?
hints: Find $c$ so that the probabilities sum to 1.
Then weight each value.
Compute $0.1\times(1+4+9+16)$.
why: The pmf must sum to 1.

stem: Monthly claims are mostly small, but a few are very large. Which relationship is typical?

options.text: The mean is below the median
options.why: Large claims pull the mean upward, not downward.
That holds for symmetric distributions.

options.text: The mode is the largest value
options.why: The mode is the most common value, here a small one.

solution: Right skew pulls the mean toward the tail while the median stays near the bulk.
hints: Which measure is sensitive to extreme values?
Large claims pull in which direction?
Compare the two measures.
why: Heavy right tails raise the mean more than the median.

stem: Project A pays ₹100 000 with probability 0.6 and loses ₹20 000 otherwise. Project B pays ₹50 000 for certain. By how much does the expected payoff of A exceed that of B?
hints: Compute the expected payoff of A.
B is certain, so its expectation is 50 000.
Take the difference.
why: The loss has probability 0.4.

stem: Exam scores have mean 62 and standard deviation 8. A student scores 78. How many standard deviations above the mean is that?
hints: Subtract the mean from the score.
Divide by the standard deviation.
Interpret in SD units.
why: A z-score of 2 means 2 SDs above the mean.

stem: Each loan application is approved with probability 0.25, independently. What is the expected number of applications needed until the first approval (counting the successful one)?
solution: For a geometric waiting time with success probability $p$, $E = 1/p = 4$.
hints: This is a geometric waiting time.
Recall the mean of a geometric variable.
Take the reciprocal of $p$.
why: Rarer success means longer waits.

stem: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the expected value of the larger of the two numbers?
hints: Count the ordered pairs for which the maximum is $m$.
There are $2m-1$ such pairs.
Weight and add.
why: The maximum is above the single-die mean of 3.5.

stem: Of 50 independent customers, each defaults with probability 0.08. What is the variance of the number of defaults?
hints: Variance of one Bernoulli indicator is $p(1-p)$.
Independent variances add.
Multiply by 50.
why: Variance is $np(1-p)$.

stem: Daily sales have mean 500 and standard deviation 40, with an unknown distribution. What is the Chebyshev upper bound on the probability that sales differ from the mean by 100 or more?
hints: Express 100 in standard deviations.
Chebyshev: bound $=1/k^2$.
Compute $1/2.5^2$.
why: Chebyshev is conservative but needs no distribution.

sub: expectation does not imply a typical outcome
stem: A lottery has expected winnings of ₹250 per ticket. Which statement is correct?

answer.display: Over many tickets the average winning per ticket tends toward ₹250, though a single ticket will rarely pay exactly that

options.text: Over many tickets the average winning per ticket tends toward ₹250, though a single ticket will rarely pay exactly that
A single ticket will usually pay about ₹250
options.why: Individual outcomes can be far from the mean.
The mean is not a guaranteed payment.

options.text: You win ₹250 at least half the time
options.why: The mean is not the median or a threshold.

solution: Expectation is a long-run average, not a typical single outcome.
It may not even be a possible value.
hints: Think of the long-run average.
Is the expected value always attainable?
Pick the statement about many tickets.
misconception: Reading the mean as a typical single outcome.
why: The mean summarises many repetitions.

sub: expected cost with fixed and variable parts
stem: A call centre has a fixed cost of ₹5 000 per day plus ₹20 per call. Calls per day have mean 300 and standard deviation 30. What are the mean and standard deviation of daily cost? Give the standard deviation.
hints: Write cost as a linear function of calls.
The fixed cost does not affect spread.
Multiply the SD by 20.
misconception: Adding the fixed cost to the SD.
why: Only the variable part scales the spread.

stem: Two independent components each last 1, 2 or 3 months with equal probability. The system fails when the first component fails. What is the expected lifetime of the system in months?
hints: Count the pairs for each possible minimum.
Weight each minimum by its probability.
Add the three terms.
why: The first failure is earlier than a typical component.
